# Tracker Creation Delegation Decision

The draft described the Unfuddle adapter as being too close to the “creation entry point.” It was written that way because the old investigation left only the issue name and call name, with the trace-back landing at `lib/issue_trackers/apis/unfuddle.rb`. That was enough to locate the relevant code, but not enough to prove that all creation actions were handled by that file.

The two objects should still be considered separately. The issue tracker creation boundary is concerned with which segment initiates the action from the point where an issue needs to be created to the handoff to the tracker integration, and which segment only passes along an existing object. Tracker template delegation is concerned with whether responsibility for template selection or rendering enters the adapter together with the creation action. Combining the two would cause “a creation-related name appears in the path” to be misread as “the template is also handled here.”

The draft's “for now, treat it as being close to the creation entry point” should remain an old judgment and should no longer be treated as implementation ownership. The available material only shows that this path is an existing Ruby module that can be used for code reading and historical behavior checks; there is no complete call chain or record of how the template object is created or passed out.

Three ways of organizing this were compared at the time:

1. Combine the creation boundary and template delegation into one adapter item. The page would be shorter, but during regression it would be impossible to tell whether the reader was stuck on the creation action or the template description.
2. Directly designate the Unfuddle file as the implementation owner for both pieces of work. This is the simplest wording, but it treats the file location as reference verification.
3. Keep the two objects separate, use this file as the starting point for the old investigation, and limit the ownership conclusion to the local relationships that have been checked.

The second option was not adopted. The first was not adopted either, because the two objects expose different issues during regression: the creation boundary requires the missing steps to be restored according to the actual user flow, while template delegation requires checking whether someone who did not participate in the changes can follow the documentation as originally intended. The third option was chosen.

The review of the materials for TRC-206 left a record of the checks; afterward, the shared test environment was temporarily unavailable. This blocker did not produce a new ownership conclusion. After the handoff confirmation for TRC-212, the quality materials reviewed the behavior boundary through the existing issue tracker integration entry point; this shows that regression was scheduled and reviewed, but cannot by itself prove that template delegation has been narrowed to the Unfuddle adapter.

The standing decision is that the creation boundary remains a separate object, and template delegation remains an adjacent object. When reading `lib/issue_trackers/apis/unfuddle.rb`, you can trace back from creation-related calls, but you cannot merge template ownership into this file solely because of its filename, module location, or the name used in the old investigation.

If an actual reference is added, change only the segment that has been confirmed: the handoff point for the creation action or the actual destination of template delegation. Do not use completion of one item as a reason to rewrite the historical record of the other.

# Tracker Creation and Delegation Decision

Old links still bring “issue tracker creation boundary” and “tracker template delegation” to this page. The two requirements are in the same memo not because they have been proven to be part of the same implementation, but because when Cascade 4.2 was being closed out, both happened to be questioned along the issue tracker integration path. Looking back later revealed that the earliest wording made “you can start looking here” sound like “the work is completed here.” This distinction needs to remain.

The scope of this page has always been narrow: it covers only the creation boundary, template delegation, and why the old investigation landed on `lib/issue_trackers/apis/unfuddle.rb`. It does not provide a complete explanation of the tracker integration, nor does it summarize template formats, fields, or other adapters. DOC-17 records another set of interface review materials; the two pages being adjacent only means that both were surfaced during the stabilization window at the time, not that they share the same implementation judgment.

## Original Record: Two Different Ways of Asking the Question

The decision recorded in the first version was not to merge the creation boundary and template delegation into a single “tracker flow” item. That division has not been withdrawn. The question for the creation boundary is: at what point does the issue end its responsibility between needing to be created and being handed off to the integration? The question for template delegation is: does template selection or rendering get handed off elsewhere along with this action? Both questions contain “tracker,” but they are tracking different objects.

The draft at the time also included: “For now, handle this through the Unfuddle file near the creation entry point.” That sentence should remain in the old version because it explains the direction of the early investigation. The old record contained only the issue name and call name, and both led people to `lib/issue_trackers/apis/unfuddle.rb`. Without more local references, treating that module as the first stop was a reasonable working arrangement; treating it as the final owner of the creation action exceeded what the record at the time could support.

The early text did not make this provisional status clear. It required checking creation-related calls along the adapter before deciding whether the template should be documented in the same place. The sequence itself was not a problem; the problem was that “near the entry point” was later read as “the entry point has already been located.” The old record is not being deleted because many regression notes still use that path; however, it can no longer support a judgment about implementation responsibility on its own.

## Wording Excluded at Closeout

During closeout, merging the two objects into one item was discussed. The advantage was a shorter page, with readers needing to remember only “tracker creation.” This wording was not adopted, not for the sake of tidy categorization, but because real-world problems would occur in different places: some people could not find the creation step by following the actual flow; others could reach the creation action but would not know who continued handling the template documentation. A merged title would conflate these two ways of getting stuck.

Another option was to list the Unfuddle adapter as the implementation owner for both tasks. It looked more explicit than the first option and had also appeared in early verbal retellings. It was not written as a decision later because the current materials provide only the local responsibilities and adjacent navigation for this Ruby module. The file exists, the old investigation can start here, and the module name is related to the issue tracker; all three statements are true. Directly inferring from them that template delegation is implemented here, however, skips the reference relationships that need to be checked.

The final decision retained was the narrower one: keep the two objects documented separately; use the Unfuddle file as the recheck point for the old investigation; write in the actual handoff locations for the creation action and template handling only after the corresponding references have been verified. This decision does not put the issue aside; it refuses to use one term as a substitute for two objects still requiring verification. For the closeout at the time, it was more important to let regression identify which segment was missing than to give an overly broad ownership conclusion.

## Retained Old Approach

> Old approach: infer from the adapter name that creation and templates are both on the same side, and retain only one entry point in the documentation.
>
> This approach was not formally adopted. It remains here because it explains why the old links, old investigation, and initial draft repeatedly pointed to the same file. It is no longer suitable as a new regression baseline.

This old approach can easily create a false impression when read. The adapter path is indeed a concrete object, not an abstract label; however, the path may also merely take the reader to a local declaration or an adjacent call. The creation boundary may be confirmed near that module, or it may only become complete by starting from the location that calls it. The same applies to template delegation. The fact that both objects can be investigated from the same place does not mean that they end at the same place.

The “unified explanation” after the old approach has not been carried forward either. This page no longer requires creation, templates, and all tracker-related terms to be gathered into one paragraph. What needs to be added is either a missing creation step in a real user flow or the destination lost while reading a piece of template delegation documentation; the two types of additions should each be returned to their corresponding object.

## Recheck Diagram for the Old Investigation

The diagram only shows the two verification paths branching from one file location in the old investigation; it does not represent the execution order of the creation action or template handling.

```mermaid
stateDiagram-v2
  state "Unfuddle Recheck Point" as unfuddle
  state "Creation Boundary To Be Confirmed" as creation
  state "Template Delegation To Be Confirmed" as template
  [*] --> unfuddle
  unfuddle --> creation
  unfuddle --> template
```

This diagram preserves the way the search was conducted at the time. It must not be read as saying that the template definitely leaves from that module, nor as saying that the creation action definitely ends at that module. The two paths are parallel because the old record brought both questions to the same recheck point; they should subsequently be used to find the creation handoff and the destination of the template separately.

## After the Cards Returned

TRC-206 brought the creation boundary back into the real user flow. The card required filling in the missing step by going through one flow, rather than expanding the background further. This changes how the page is used: when arriving at the Unfuddle file from an old link, looking only at the module name and historical notes is not enough; it is also necessary to see where the flow changes from “needs to be created” to “handed off to the integration.” Until this step is filled in, the file location cannot be treated as the flow boundary.

A review of the materials in September confirmed that the documentation had been revisited. The shared test environment then became temporarily unavailable, and the review produced no further material that could be used to broaden the conclusion. There was previously a view that an unavailable environment affected only regression and not the ownership determination. In retrospect, that wording was too light: ownership had not been determined by the path in the first place, and the environment issue neither made it clearer nor provided new evidence for template delegation.

TRC-212 returned template delegation to hands-on regression. After the handoff was confirmed, the quality materials reviewed the behavior boundary through the existing entry point for the issue tracker integration. This should be read as a second look at the materials and entry point, not as proof that “the template has already been handed over to Unfuddle.” The card required readers who had not participated in the changes to follow the instructions and record the pages and links where they got stuck. This shows that the template issue still needs to be exposed by whether the instructions can be followed end to end, rather than having the adapter name decide the conclusion for it.

The relationship between the two cards must not be interpreted in reverse either. The flow-step restoration required by TRC-206 cannot replace the delegation documentation in TRC-212; the hands-on reading in TRC-212 cannot replace reference verification for the creation action. They are both retained on this page only so that readers arriving from the old record can distinguish whether the next step is to return to the flow or to the template documentation.

## Where the Path Should Be Retained

`lib/issue_trackers/apis/unfuddle.rb` should continue to appear in the recheck notes. It is the specific location already used by the old investigation and is associated with the local module for issue tracker API. Deleting the path would remove the entry point from the old record and could make later readers think there was originally no basis at all. Retaining the path does not expand its evidentiary force.

When reading this file, it is reasonable to look for creation-related calls first, because that is the clue left by the old investigation. If local references show that an object is passed onward from here, record that transfer location under the creation boundary; if references show that the template is taken over elsewhere, record that destination under template delegation. Conversely, if all that was found was a declaration, naming, or adjacent navigation, record only “rechecked up to here,” and do not rewrite it as “responsible here.”

The old version placed “actual relationships still take precedence from references” next to the path, which read like a generic reservation. This revision grounds it in two specific questions: the creation boundary requires confirmation of the creation action’s handoff; template delegation requires confirmation of where template handling goes. Without one of these two local relationships, the page can retain the historical judgment but cannot supply a new implementation conclusion.

## Narrow Convention for Template Delegation

“Template delegation” on this page should not be expanded to include all presentation, all fields, or all notification content. What remains here is only a responsibility question: does the side where the creation action occurs continue to handle the template, or is it handed elsewhere? Without supporting material, do not add a name to the template, do not speculate about rendering order, and do not attribute every page issue encountered by readers to the template.

Accordingly, the wording “the template naturally follows after creation is complete” is no longer used. It once made the record appear coherent, but it turned an unchecked connection into an established fact. If a later review confirms only the boundary of the creation action, update only the creation portion of this page; if it confirms only the destination of the template, correct only the template portion. The two may ultimately connect, but they must be connected by actual relationships, not by documentation wording.

## Questions Still Not Consolidated

- When tracing inward from the old path, the exact point where the creation action is handed to the tracker integration still needs to be confirmed through reference relationships.
- Whether template handling is at the same location as that handoff, or is handled later by another object, has not been settled in the materials on this page.
- Whether the flow step required to be restored by TRC-206 and the pages and links where readers got stuck in TRC-212 point to the same break point cannot be determined from the titles of the two cards alone.

These questions remain not to withdraw the decision. What has been decided is the recording method: do not merge the objects, do not elevate the historical recheck path into an ownership assignment, and ensure that later additions land precisely in either the creation handoff or the template destination. The old page still has reference value because it preserves why the investigation initially started from the Unfuddle adapter; it is not suitable for directly assigning current implementation responsibility.

When someone updates this page later, they should retain the initial draft’s wording “near the creation entry point” and its correction. Removing it would make the old links appear baseless and would erase a real change in judgment. New material only needs to answer one specific question: where is the creation action handed off, or where does the template handling go? As long as the answer stops at a filename, module name, or old investigation label, continue to place it in the recheck record rather than writing it into the decision itself.

# Deployment Contract Compatibility Migration Notes

## The Entry Point Left by the Old Page

This page did not originally start with deployment scripts. The old investigation followed issue names and call names, eventually stopping at `config/initializers/devise.rb`. The file index provided only a local entry point into an existing rb module, useful for reading code and checking historical behavior; it did not connect Capistrano's deployment actions, Unicorn's startup actions, or the actual call edges between them.

The old page interpreted this stopping point as the place where the deployment contract was implemented. The only terms visible at the time were `application`, `config`, `env`, `default`, and `timeout`. These terms were enough to suggest looking at configuration initialization first, but not enough to prove who wrote a value, which process read it, or whether the deployment steps were the same before and after the upgrade. The old page did not make this limitation clear, so later readers could easily mistake the file location for ownership of the implementation.

Retain the old assessment: after the Capistrano upgrade, the Unicorn side might still read values in the old initialization order; if deployment results regress, first restore the pre-upgrade deployment combination, then check the initialization file. This assessment was not supported by actual calls, logs, or user outcomes at the time. It remains here as a historical assessment, not recast as a definitive conclusion today.

```text
Old investigation: issue name / call name
              |
              v
config/initializers/devise.rb
              |
              ?  application / config / env / default / timeout

Migration target: not confirmed on this page
Rollback entry point: the pre-upgrade Capistrano and Unicorn combination (specific files not recorded)
```

## Operational Excerpt from v1

The sequence actually written in the old draft was short:

1. First preserve the pre-upgrade Capistrano configuration.
2. Compare the configuration values and default values in the deployment environment.
3. Check whether Unicorn still reads from the same initialization entry point at startup.
4. Then perform deployment and process startup.

These four steps describe the working hypothesis at the time, not a migration that had already been successfully completed. In particular, step 3 had no corresponding call snippet, and step 4 left no deployment output either. The old draft stated that “initialization in the same place” was a condition for the contract to hold, but did not say who was responsible for confirming it. Looking back now, only the verification entry point and the items still to be supplied can be confirmed; the implementation relationship involving Capistrano or Unicorn cannot be inferred from a path name.

The recovery procedure at the time was also described only at the combination level: if a regression occurs, stop further switching, restore the pre-upgrade Capistrano/Unicorn combination, then return to `config/initializers/devise.rb` to check configuration loading. No directly executable commands were recorded, nor were the specific pages, statuses, or logs that should appear after recovery. Leave this gap as it is rather than filling it with a seemingly complete command.

## Views Revised During Review

On 2025-9-24, TRC-209 moved from To Do to In Progress, with the topic still being the regression in results after the Capistrano upgrade. This action indicates that the old entry point still needed investigation, but provided no new calling method or results. By 9-26, the card had returned to To Do. The “migration target” on this page therefore remains blank: no material confirms which Capistrano configuration was being migrated to which other configuration, and no material confirms which contract the Unicorn side actually accepted.

There are two paths here that are easy to conflate:

- **Investigation path**: enter `config/initializers/devise.rb` from an issue name or call name to continue looking for references.
- **Deployment path**: Capistrano deploys and has Unicorn use the configuration; the specific files and sequence have not yet been reconstructed.

The old page drew these as a single line. After review, they can only be preserved separately. The investigation path is navigation that was actually left behind; the deployment path is still an incomplete migration record. Do not describe the initialization file as the sole owner of the deployment contract just because both paths appear on the same page.

## Migration Batches

This page has no batch numbers that can be checked, nor deployment results for each batch. To avoid expanding one upgrade regression into a fictional deployment history, only a table that can be filled in further is retained for now:

| Batch | What is known | Material still needed |
| --- | --- | --- |
| The regression after the Capistrano upgrade | The outcome occurred, and the issue was taken up again in TRC-209 | Configurations before and after the upgrade, actual calls, results seen by users |
| Other deployments | No records on this page | Do not infer batches or success status from the title |

If actual calls become available later, first place them beside the existing event in the first row, then explain whether the calls read environment values, default values, or values after initialization. Only then can we determine whether the change during migration from the old path to the new path occurred in the deployment tool, Unicorn startup, or application initialization. “The configuration has been unified” cannot currently substitute for this step.

## Two Recovery Paths

### Only Configuration Value Changes Found

Stop at configuration comparison first; do not continue switching processes. Preserve the pre-upgrade Capistrano configuration and deployment artifacts, and record the differences between `env`, `default`, and the actual read location. Without call snippets, the differences cannot be attributed to Unicorn. For recovery, return to the pre-upgrade deployment combination; the specific recovery files were not preserved in the old records.

### Startup Order Changes Found

If later investigation confirms that Unicorn startup did not follow the old initialization order, first preserve the post-upgrade state, then restore the pre-upgrade order and combination. Do not directly delete the entry point at `config/initializers/devise.rb`, or change it into a new shared configuration location; this page contains no such migration decision. Checks after recovery should at least identify where the configuration was read and the connection between the deployment results and the regression.

### Only an Issue Name Is Visible, with No Calls

In this case, follow the old investigation path into `config/initializers/devise.rb`, but stop at file declarations or adjacency relationships. An issue name can help locate a candidate entry point, but cannot prove that a call occurred. Retain the regression description in the card and wait for actual calls and user outcomes; do not write “no calls” when the finding is “not found.”

## Boundaries Between the Old and New Paths

“Old path” has two meanings on this page. One is the pre-upgrade Capistrano/Unicorn deployment combination; the other is the old investigation entry point that leads from issue names and call names back to the initialization file. Neither has a complete file list. The so-called “new path” also has only a provisional direction: continue using `config/initializers/devise.rb` as the starting point for verification while supplying the actual deployment calls. It is not an approved new deployment method.

The migration therefore cannot be executed as a fixed set of actions such as “copy the old configuration, replace the version, restart Unicorn.” The input contains no actual records of these actions; writing them out directly would pass off standard practice as what happened in this incident. The only operations that can be retained are: preserve the old combination, check configuration sources, and confirm the relationship between startup and configuration reads; if a regression is found, stop before switching and restore the old combination.

## The Old Description of Responsibility Boundaries

The old page assumed that the initialization file was the place closest to the issue, and that compatibility between Capistrano and Unicorn could be assessed there in one pass. This is the obsolete part, retained for those who need to understand the historical assessment. This file can serve as an entry point for tracing back, but this page has no evidence assigning it responsibility for deployment, process management, or writing environment variables.

If further investigation continues, the person responsible for verification should separately record: how the issue name points to the file, which declaration in the file connects to `application` or `config`, and how the deployment process passes values to Unicorn. Without the latter two of these three parts, the page can only record navigation, not assign deployment responsibility. No responsible parties are supplied here on behalf of other projects or other pages.

## Actionable Stopping Points at This Stage

- No actual calls found: stop at `config/initializers/devise.rb`, add TODO, and do not declare the migration complete.
- Only configuration differences: preserve the old configuration and post-upgrade state, and do not switch the next batch yet.
- Regression confirmed to come from the upgraded combination: restore the pre-upgrade Capistrano/Unicorn combination, then preserve the regression results.
- Only a card status change: treat it as work progress, not compatibility verification.

TRC-209 moving back from In Progress to To Do corresponds exactly to the last case. It neither closed out the old assessment nor produced a new contract. The current page therefore retains the old path, the old rollback description, and the unfinished addition of actual calls; if material becomes available later, append it directly after the relevant paragraph rather than reorganizing this page into a new deployment specification.

# Decision on the Webhook Issue Object

The initial draft retained `public/javascripts/notifier.js` and limited its role to an entry point for the earlier investigation. That assessment remains valid. Later, TRC-215 was linked to a support record; the to-do item on the card was still to find a caller that was still using the “Webhook issue object” and verify its actual version, entry point, and current result. The link itself did not provide a request body sample, nor did it connect the file to external notification delivery.

A later note on the card requested that it remain open for now because one aspect of external notification delivery was still unconfirmed. The card then moved to In Progress. These changes indicate that the issue had returned to the integration investigation; they do not establish object fields, a sending location, or runtime results.

## What the Old Entry Point Can Establish

The code identified so far is still limited to this short snippet:

```js
function printStackTrace(options) {
  var ex = options.e || null, guess = !!options.guess;
}
```

`ex` is a local value obtained from `options.e`, and `guess` is a Boolean switch derived from `options.guess`. The function name points to traceback printing, so it is not surprising that the earlier investigation reached this file through an exception issue.

Previously, someone casually interpreted the “exception object” as the “Webhook issue object.” That interpretation is now retained as an unverified earlier assessment. It came from the proximity of the function name, variable name, and issue name, rather than evidence about the call. If that proximity is recorded as establishing where the object belongs, then once the actual sending boundary is discovered, it will be impossible to distinguish established relationships from what was merely conjecture at the time.

What can be recorded from the file is: the earlier investigation passed through here; the file contains `printStackTrace(options)`; and that function reads two local options. What cannot be recorded from the file is: the Webhook recipient, request body shape, object source, delivery timing, or whether the current call still passes through this module.

## Choices During the Stable Window

The choice at the time was not between “continue investigating” and “stop investigating,” but between several different ways of recording the findings.

| Choice | Treatment of the Old Path | What Is Gained | What Is Given Up |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Make a definitive classification | Record `notifier.js` as the object's implementation location | Quickly establish a single entry point | Would expand function-local inputs into a claim about where the interface belongs |
| Keep only the name | Remove the file and function clues | Avoid mistaking the file for the definition | Cannot explain why the earlier investigation turned to the exception module |
| Retain and narrow the scope | Retain the path and snippet, and require finding the caller first | Historical clues remain available for review | Cannot immediately provide an object specification |

The third option was chosen. The file path may continue to appear, but references to it must carry the context of an “entry point for the earlier investigation.” It is neither an assertion of the current implementation location nor a source for the Webhook object's fields.

This decision does not rule out either of two future outcomes: new evidence about the call may show that the file participates in object construction, or it may show that the file only handles exception display or tracebacks. In either case, the old record does not need to be deleted; it only needs to be placed back at the level of the historical investigation, rather than used as evidence for the current call.

## Separating the Terminology

In the stable-window materials, “Webhook issue object” refers to at least several different levels. Combining these levels into a single statement produces assessments that cannot be verified.

| Role of the Name in the Materials | What Is Known | What Is Still Missing |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Investigation topic | TRC-215 uses this name to organize integration issues | Whether the name corresponds to a fixed request body structure |
| Historical navigation | The old record points to `public/javascripts/notifier.js` | Whether the file belongs to the current notification chain |
| Local function | `printStackTrace(options)` can be located | Whether the function constructs the issue object |
| Current caller | The card requires the search to continue | Actual location, version, entry point, and result |
| External notification delivery | One aspect remains unconfirmed | At which boundary the unconfirmed item occurs |

This breakdown is not a specification table. It only defines where new evidence should be recorded. If a call location is found, add the call location; if a runtime result is obtained, add the result; discuss the request body only after obtaining evidence about the sending boundary. Facts already available in one column cannot be used to fill gaps in another.

## Order of Operations

The follow-up investigation will proceed in the following order:

1. Use the issue name in TRC-215 to find a caller that is still in use.
2. Confirm the actual version at that caller. The old record contains `v_prev` with `internal/TRACE`; this cannot automatically be carried over to the new location.
3. Record the entry point that leads into the call; do not infer the entry point from the function name.
4. Record one current result, distinguishing “the code location was found” from “the object actually reached the boundary that needs investigation.”
5. Only then check whether there is a direct relationship between the caller and `notifier.js`.

Step 5 is placed last to prevent the old file from driving the current investigation. Continuing to read adjacent code in the same file can, at most, improve local understanding of the module; it cannot replace confirmation of the current integration.

If no caller can be found in the first step, the investigation stops at the first step. Do not invent a most likely call location based on the old path. If only another piece of exception-handling code is found, it can only serve as a new local clue; it does not count as having found the object's caller.

If a caller is found but its version is unknown, simply record the location and the version gap; do not fill in `v_prev` at that location. If both the version and entry point are available but a current result is still missing, the object still cannot be recorded as having passed through external notification delivery.

## Current Decision

Maintain the approach of “retain the old path, do not determine where the implementation belongs prematurely, and prioritize the current caller.”

TRC-215 remains an entry point for the investigation. The support-record link and card status changes indicate that the issue is still being worked on; they cannot replace evidence about the call. If a direct connection between the file and the current caller is later discovered, add the connection itself; if the two are confirmed to be unrelated, still retain the historical fact that the old path was part of the investigation.

DOC-22 discusses localization of English error counts and can serve as navigation to related materials, but it provides no evidence for the Webhook object's source or delivery.

# Webhook Issue Object Decision

At the start of the stability window, “Webhook issue object” was a name sufficient to make people start searching, but insufficient to let them reach an implementation conclusion. The earliest surviving investigation clue brought the issue name and call name to `public/javascripts/notifier.js`. This location was never deleted afterward because it did explain the reading path at the time; however, it repeatedly led to the same misreading: seeing an exception-related function and treating it as the source of the external notification object.

The decision preserved on this page does not attempt to define a complete interface for Webhook. It addresses a more specific tradeoff in the stability window: given an identifiable old file, an unconfirmed object name, and a card that has re-entered processing, which relationships can remain, and which relationships must wait to be written until the current caller appears.

TRC-215 is the card entry point for this page. When the card was created, the observation was “Webhook issue object integrated into the routine usage workflow”; the local to-do required finding the caller still using this object and verifying the actual version, entry point, and current result. A support record was later linked to the card, followed by an addendum requesting that it not be closed for now because one aspect of external notification delivery remained unconfirmed. The card entering In Progress indicates that the investigation was picked up again; it did not provide an object sample or replace the call location.

## The Earliest File Lead

The old investigation pointed to the file `public/javascripts/notifier.js`. The snippet that can currently be located directly in that file is small:

```js
function printStackTrace(options) {
  var ex = options.e || null, guess = !!options.guess;
}
```

There are two local facts here. `printStackTrace` receives `options`; the function reads `options.e` into `ex` and converts `options.guess` into the boolean value `guess`. The function name and traceback printout are adjacent, so it is not surprising that an exception issue led to this location.

But this snippet contains no request-body construction, sending action, recipient, or field description for the “Webhook issue object.” `ex` is the exception value used by the function; it does not become a property of the notification object merely because the names are similar. `guess` is a local switch; it does not become a delivery condition merely because it appears in the file. Locating the file and locating the object are two different things.

The earliest work notes did contain an easy assumption: since the function handles an exception, the issue object might simply be the exception description here. This interpretation was not deleted because it explains why the old investigation stopped at the browser-side js module; however, it is no longer used as a basis for judgment. It skipped the most critical link: how local exception handling becomes external notification content, whether it becomes such content at all, and where.

> Previous assessment: the issue object might be the exception description used by `printStackTrace`.
>
> Current interpretation: this function is only sufficient to show that the earlier investigation examined exception-related code; it cannot establish the source of the Webhook object.

This correction does not mean that the old entry point has no value. Quite the opposite: the entry point is still worth retaining because it was an investigation path that was actually followed. What has been withdrawn is the wording that elevates that path into a claim about where the implementation belongs.

## What needed to be decided at the time

During the stabilization window, there was a seemingly convenient approach: first organize the “issue object” into field descriptions, then pick possible fields from exception-related code to fill them in. This could quickly produce a page that looked like an interface definition, but if the fields were merely inferred from `options.e`, `options.guess`, or function names, it would turn speculation into long-term fact.

Another approach was to delete the old file entirely and retain only the issue name. This would prevent anyone from mistaking `notifier.js` for the definition location again, but it would also leave those taking over later unable to understand why an old document discussing external notifications turned toward traceback-printing code. A historical entry point becoming invalid and a historical entry point that should never have existed are different situations; deleting the path must not blur the distinction between them.

The stabilization window therefore involved comparing three options:

| Option | Treatment of the old path | Benefit | Cost |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Assign a definitive classification directly | Record `notifier.js` as the implementation location of the Webhook object | Provides a single entry point immediately | Local variables would be mistaken for object fields, and the file location would be mistaken for the component responsible for sending |
| Retain only the name | Delete the file and function references, and write only the issue name | Avoids misreading which file owns the implementation | The actual course of the earlier investigation cannot be traced back |
| Retain and narrow the interpretation | Retain the path, function, and local snippets, and first examine current callers | Historical clues remain usable, and conclusions stay within the evidence | An object specification cannot be produced immediately |

The decision was to adopt the third option.

This decision does not mean that `notifier.js` is necessarily unrelated to Webhook, nor does it mean that it is already unrelated. It only stipulates that, without caller evidence, “the old record once jumped here” cannot be rewritten as “the object is implemented here.” If a later investigation finds that this file participates in constructing the current object, that connection should be added; if it finds that the file serves only exception display or tracebacks, that result should also be recorded, while retaining the context that the earlier investigation reached this file.

## Different objects under the same name

The “Webhook issue object” served more than one role in the stabilization-window materials. If they are written as objects at the same level, unverifiable statements naturally emerge, such as “the object is generated in notifier,” “the object enters external notifications,” or “the object is the exception description.” These statements may refer respectively to an issue name, a code location, a runtime boundary, or a request body, but no materials connect these levels into a single established fact.

The current record uses the following breakdown:

| Where the name appears | Meaning on this page | Content that can already be recorded | Content that still cannot be recorded |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Card subject | Search name for the integration investigation | TRC-215 Continue working on this object | Whether the name corresponds to a fixed JSON structure |
| Old investigation path | Code location inspected at the time | `public/javascripts/notifier.js` | Whether it belongs to the current sending chain |
| Local function | Declaration that can be located in the file | `printStackTrace(options)` reads `e` and `guess` | Whether it constructs or delivers the issue object |
| Current caller | Location where the object is still in use | The card requires continued searching | The location, version, entry point, and result are not yet complete |
| External notification delivery | Scope newly identified in the addendum | One item is unconfirmed, so the card cannot be closed | Where the unconfirmed item occurred and what result it produced |
| Request body object | Content requiring confirmation of the material at the sending boundary | This page has no field material yet | Fields, shape, and source |

This is not a field comparison table. Its purpose is to prevent new material from being recorded in the wrong place. Once the call location is found, record it under “Current caller”; once the version is confirmed, record only the version at that call location; only after obtaining a result once should you record the version and entry point to which the result applies. Do not use local variables from an old file to fill in the request body, and do not write a card status transition as the result of a single run.

After these layers are separated, the old path is neither treated as invalid noise nor elevated to evidence about the object. It retains its role as historical navigation; locating the object requires an entry point that is still in use and can account for the version, entry method, and current result.

## Restrictions after the card was processed again

After the support record was linked to TRC-215, the tone of the investigation changed once. The initial draft only left “caller to be found”; after the link was made, external notification delivery was explicitly retained as an unconfirmed area. We cannot go further than that here: linking does not mean that a delivery sample has already been obtained, nor does it mean that a known failure definitely occurred at the sending end. It only suffices to show that this gap still affects the integration assessment and is not something that can be automatically archived according to old notes.

The addendum saying “don’t close it yet” has the same boundary. It does not state that the object is definitely missing, that the format has definitely changed, or that the old js file definitely did not participate. It only prevents us from writing the existing clues as proof that external notification delivery has been fully investigated. Rewriting the status rationale as a technical attribution would create another layer of certainty without a source.

The card then entered in-progress status, indicating that someone had started handling it. Processing status is not a result. The minimum requirements left by the card remain the same set of items: a caller that is still in use, the actual version it uses, the entry point into that call, and the current result. As long as any one of these has not been found, it cannot be written as “object definition confirmed”.

This limitation avoids two kinds of rework. The first is guessing the interface based on an old js file, then throwing out the entire section after finding the actual call site. The second is seeing that the support record is already linked and writing “the issue appeared again” as “the delivery has been reproduced.” The latter is the one that must be avoided most during the stable window, because external notifications can span multiple locations, while the current material confirms only one location that remains unconfirmed.

## Processing Order

The order in the initial draft is still valid, but the subsequent review states the stopping point for each step more clearly.

1. Use the problem name from TRC-215 to find callers that are still in use.
2. Once one is found, first confirm the actual version. The old-file reference is the `v_prev` with `internal/TRACE`; that marker belongs only to the old investigation entry point and cannot naturally become the version of the new call site.
3. Record the entry point into the call. The entry point should describe where the location is actually reached from, rather than inferring a chain from the function name.
4. Record one current result. The result must correspond to the previously confirmed call site and version before it can show whether the object actually reaches the boundary that requires investigation.
5. Only then compare the relationship between that caller and `public/javascripts/notifier.js`.

Putting the old-file relationship last is not because the adjacent code has no reading value. Continuing to read within the same file can improve local understanding of this module; it cannot resolve the gap of whether the current integration passes through here. If a great deal of effort is first spent inside the file, the page will gradually turn into a note tracing functions and reading code, instead obscuring that the original issue remains the integration status of the external notification object.

The diagram below shows only the verification order adopted by this decision; it does not indicate that a complete call chain has already been found:

```mermaid
stateDiagram-v2
  state "Old investigation entry point\npublic/javascripts/notifier.js" as old_path
  state "Caller still in use, pending confirmation" as caller
  state "Actual version pending verification" as version
  state "Entry point pending verification" as entry
  state "Current result pending verification" as result
  [*] --> old_path
  old_path --> caller
  caller --> version
  version --> entry
  entry --> result
```

If the first step does not find a caller, the investigation stops there. Do not reconstruct a “most likely” caller from the old path, and do not treat another block of exception-handling code as an equivalent substitute. If only the old entry point and a local function have been confirmed, the conclusion stops at “confirmed the old entry point and local function.”

If a call site is found but the version is unknown, record the location and the version gap. Do not insert the old entry point into the new location just because it carries `v_prev`. When the version is unknown, the call site is still a valuable new fact, but it is not sufficient to support a judgment about the current behavior.

If both the version and the entry point are available but there is not even one current result, the record should stop at “location and entry method identified.” This means the investigation has moved one step beyond the old path; it does not mean the object has reached the external notification boundary. This distinction is especially important once the support record reappears: the support association proves that the issue is worth investigating further, but does not itself provide a result.

Only when all four items are complete is it appropriate to revisit where the old file participates. At that point, there are two equally valuable possible outcomes: the call materials link the old file to the object, or the call materials show that the old file only explains the historical investigation and did not participate in the current integration. Both outcomes are more reliable than inferring object ownership directly from the function name.

## Shortcuts Abandoned

### Turning Function Parameters into Object Fields

Someone once suggested first writing `e` and `guess` as the core fields of the issue object and filling in the rest later. This approach was not adopted. `options.e` and `options.guess` are local options read by the function, and the existing material does not put them in the Webhook request body. If they are added to the field table, it becomes difficult for readers to tell that they came from function parameters rather than from the sent object.

This wording also has a practical cost: subsequent investigation will tend to verify the fields set in advance instead of first confirming the object boundary. The stability window does not use the order of “define the fields first, then find the entry point.”

### Replacing the External Notification Investigation with Exception Display

The old path is in an existing js module, and the function name points to stack-trace printing, so someone argued that the card topic should be downgraded to a frontend exception display issue. This classification was not adopted either. The creation observation for TRC-215 is still part of the integration flow, and the later addendum still points to external notification delivery. One old file alone cannot change the investigation topic to something else.

Conversely, the presence of Webhook in the topic does not allow us to assert that the old module is definitely the wrong entry point. The existing material is insufficient to make this either-or determination. The current decision requires the two lines to be recorded separately until the actual call relationship links them or clearly establishes that they are separate.

### Waiting Until All Materials Are Complete Before Retaining the Decision

Another view was to take down this page first and rewrite the explanation after the complete chain was found. That was not done. The stability window itself needs to preserve the choices already made: why the old path was retained, why it was not directly upgraded to implementation ownership, and why the card was not closed because of the existing clues. Deleting these judgments would cause the next investigation to fall into the same misinterpretation again.

Therefore, the page remains, but it is not a Webhook specification page. It records what the investigation may rely on to continue when materials are insufficient, and which shortcuts have already been abandoned.

## Two textual corrections

The first correction concerns the wording “the legacy path proves the interface.” After review, it should read “the legacy path proves that the earlier investigation once reached this file.” The former wording turns a location into implementation ownership; the latter preserves only the navigation fact. The latter wording is authoritative for now.

The second correction concerns the wording “the support association indicates reproduction.” The card’s support-association record can only show that the issue re-entered the integration investigation; the addendum still retains one unconfirmed point concerning external notification delivery. The current record uses “unconfirmed” and does not describe it as “reproduced” or “located.”

Neither correction deleted any clues. `notifier.js` is still on this page, and the support association is also still on this page. What changed was the way clues were expanded into conclusions.

## Boundary with adjacent materials

DOC-22 discuss localization of English error counts. The two pages can navigate to each other, but the localized text does not provide the source of the Webhook object and should not be used to infer the sending boundary of external notifications. The two topics are not merged here because they use different investigation subjects.

This page also does not cover a complete code walkthrough of the exception-display module. The function snippets confirmed in the file are sufficient to explain the entry point of the earlier investigation; without new call-site material, continuing to list adjacent code will not advance the object investigation. If a systematic explanation of `notifier.js` is needed in the future, it should have separate material targeted at that module, rather than expanding this decision into a code tour.

## Current decision and addendum method

The current decision remains unchanged: `public/javascripts/notifier.js` is the location reached by the earlier investigation of the “Webhook issue object”; the local declaration confirmable in the file is `printStackTrace(options)`, and it reads `options.e` and `options.guess`. These details support historical navigation and local understanding of the function, but do not support identifying this file as the implementation owner of the Webhook request body or issue object.

TRC-215 continue to serve as an investigation entry point. Some part of external notification delivery remains unconfirmed, so this investigation cannot be closed merely because the legacy path exists, the support record has been linked, or the card has moved to in progress. Future judgments should first identify the caller still in use, and then confirm the actual version, entry point, and current result at that caller.

The next addendum does not need to rewrite the entire page. When the caller is provided, add its location and indicate whether the version has been verified; when a version is provided, add it only at the corresponding location; when the entry point is provided, state clearly where the call originates; when the current result is provided, identify the call location and version to which it corresponds. Only when the direct relationship between the legacy file and the current caller is provided should an explanation connecting the two be added.

The core trade-off left by the initial draft still holds: the historical entry point may be retained, but it cannot vouch for the current integration. This stopping point is not an empty conclusion. It narrows the objects to look for next to the actual callers, and it also narrows the places most likely to be miswritten to the connections that have not yet been established among legacy files, function-local variables, support associations, and external delivery.

# Error Count Localization Plan

Initially, `config/initializers/devise.rb` was treated only as the lookup entry, with a preference for moving the sentence into the English translation. Later review did not establish that the initialization file owns the copy, so this remains a direction to try, not a decision that has been completed. What needs to be protected is the singular/plural result seen by callers, not the wording in a particular file.

### Trial scope

Start by recording two outputs at the existing entry: the English singular sentence when count is 1, and the plural sentence when count is greater than 1. The candidate text to retain is:

```text
%{count} error has
%{count} errors have
```

Here, `%{count}` must continue to be provided by the caller. The trial changes only the English display layer; it does not change the email-sending flow, other keys in the authentication configuration, or the caller's arguments. If the actual output also includes a following object name or link, use the call result as the source of truth and do not turn the half-sentence in the example into new complete copy.

### Options

**Translation catalog.** First check whether the corresponding key already exists in `config/locales/en.yml`. If it does, adjust only the singular and plural values; if it does not, confirm the key name used by the caller before deciding whether to add it. The benefit is that the English text is centralized, and rollback requires reverting only the localized translation changes. The cost is that the framework's plural-branch selection must be confirmed; do not assume that `has` and `have` will switch automatically just because their key names look similar.

**Handle it in the initialization configuration.** Keep the existing concatenation location in `config/initializers/devise.rb` and fix only the branch. This may be closer to the current call path, but it keeps user-facing text tied to startup configuration and makes it harder to determine whether other callers reuse the same logic. Keep this option only if the translation catalog does not actually take over the entry point.

**Have the caller choose the full sentence.** This avoids the unknown behavior of the localization key, but duplicates the English text; adding another language or changing the prompt later would require finding multiple call sites. Do not choose this option unless review shows that neither of the two options above is the actual output location.

Do not start the check by guessing ownership from the filename. Follow the existing call chain to find where count is passed, then record 1, a value greater than 1, and zero separately. Treat zero only as a sample pending confirmation; do not pre-classify it as singular or plural. Watch for three types of failure: the interpolation appears verbatim on the page; the number changes but the verb remains fixed as `has` or `have`; or initialization loading fails and the page never reaches the count message. If the third type occurs, revert the initialization-side changes first; do not use a successful startup to paper over unverified copy.

This can reduce environment differences, but it provides no caller output and does not decide text ownership for this page. Trial records must still preserve the actual singular, plural, and zero outputs; a fixed toolchain is not evidence that the trial passed.

It has not yet been confirmed which English form zero should use, or whether other languages share the same set of count keys. If code uses the complete English sentence as a match condition, the migration cost for the translation-catalog approach will be higher than expected; retain the old output, list the affected callers, and then decide whether to switch in phases. Proceed based on the singular/plural samples only if the caller uses it solely as display text.

When rolling back, restore only the translation items added or modified in this trial. If the initialization branch was tested, restore that branch as well, without making incidental changes to adjacent configuration. Until the review is complete, this document remains a candidate proposal: the trial scope, samples, and stop conditions are settled; copy ownership, the zero form, and whether callers need to be migrated remain to be confirmed.

# Slack Attachment and Link Troubleshooting Tree

This page originally started from a rather unreliable lead. The issue name and call name led the investigation to `app/assets/javascripts/jquery.alerts.js`, so the first draft assumed this was the shared entry point for attachments and links. At the time, the symptoms were not separated: whenever something looked wrong in Slack, the investigation returned to this path. This judgment remains in the old records because it explains why several later checks looked in the wrong place; it is no longer used to assign current responsibility.

During review, do not change the check order as soon as you open the file. Copy down the observed results, then follow the tree below:

```text
The Slack message has appeared, but its display does not match expectations
├─ Only the structured attachment content is abnormal
│  ├─ The attachment is still present: save the complete request body, and first check whether the structured fields are at the same level
│  ├─ The attachment is missing: save the pre-send object, and distinguish between an attachment missing at generation time and one discarded after sending
│  └─ Only one item is missing: record the specific field name, rather than summarizing it as “the attachment is broken”
├─ The color or title looks abnormal
│  ├─ color is abnormal: save the actual value and the caller's requirement side by side
│  ├─ title is abnormal: retain the original title, and do not fill it in using the truncated text on the page
│  └─ Both are abnormal: still record them separately first, then check whether they were produced by the same call path
└─ The message has not appeared
   ├─ A pre-send object exists: continue along the sending caller
   └─ Even the pre-send object is missing: stop at the generation entry point, and do not infer a relationship from this file path

The issue link has already appeared in the attachment
├─ The link cannot be opened
│  └─ Retain the complete URL, and confirm whether it points to an issue page or an ordinary directory page
├─ The issue page opens, but the link does not land at the standard location
│  └─ Save the destination URL and the line-number anchor in two separate columns
└─ Both the destination and the location are correct
   └─ Record it as passed, and do not recheck the link because other attachment fields are abnormal
```

“Structured attachments” and “standard issue links” are two adjacent but non-equivalent objects of inspection. An attachment having content does not mean that its links conform to the standard; a link opening does not mean that the attachment fields have been preserved as specified by the original caller. The old records combined these two checks into one troubleshooting track, making it easy to stop prematurely after seeing a result at the first point. Now, if both symptoms appear at the same time, a separate original result must be retained for each; mark them as part of the same reproduction run only when both the caller and the input are the same.

### Legacy Wording Left by the Path Assessment

An old paragraph stated: “`app/assets/javascripts/jquery.alerts.js` is the implementation location for Slack attachment issues.” This sentence is retained, but it represents only the working assumption at the time. A later review did not confirm from current references that it handles attachment serialization or issue-link generation, so “pending reference verification” was added beside the investigation record. Do not treat the directory containing the file as a module boundary, and do not infer that it is responsible for Slack because its filename contains alerts.

If the check still needs to start from this path, keep the scope of each action small:

1. First inspect the local declarations and directly adjacent code related to `color` and `title` in the file.
2. Then return to the caller that produces the Slack result, and compare the pre-send object with the actual result.
3. If no direct reference can be found, stop here and record “path checked, relationship unconfirmed”; do not treat similar names found in a search as call edges.

The order of these three steps was added after review. The first draft contained only the first step, so it could explain why the matching terms appeared in the file, but not where the result came from. The past practice of treating a “matching path” as a “located entry point” has proved insufficient; it is still retained in this document to explain the source of the old judgment.

### Investigation Records for the Link Branch

When a link is abnormal, the URL itself and the location marker at the end of the URL are the easiest things to confuse. First copy the complete link that was sent; if the copied content contains only an ordinary issue-page URL, do not add an anchor based on the location displayed on the page. If the URL contains a location component after the filename, record the filename and line number separately. This kind of record distinguishes the two failures better than “the link does not conform to the standard.”

The old records did not retain a verifiable caller, nor did they provide a final result for any specific issue link. Therefore, no particular link can be declared fixed here. The original pending investigation items in TRC-223 still apply: find a caller that still uses “Slack standard issue links,” and verify its actual version, entry point, and result. Once found, first write the caller version into the investigation copy, then return to assess whether this old path is relevant. Do not substitute the card name in TRC-223 for evidence about the caller.

### Retained Judgments for the Attachment Branch

Attachment checks deal only with the structure visible in Slack output. If the attachment exists but its field contents are wrong, save the differences between the pre-send object and the result; if the attachment never appears, first confirm whether it already existed during generation. Whether a link opens cannot substitute for an attachment check, and an attachment displaying normally cannot prove that the issue link lands at the standard location.

TRC-219 is suitable as navigation to the attachment entry point, but it only leaves the requirement to “verify the current version's behavior and identify entry points where checking can continue.” It does not provide an implementation relationship that can be copied directly back into the record. The review records therefore use a three-part “result—caller—path” format: the result is the content actually seen in Slack, the caller is the confirmed location that produced that content, and the path is elevated to an entry point only when the reference relationship can be established. If any of the three is missing, stop at the corresponding branch.

### On-Call Margin Notes Still Retained

- When the same message has both attachment and link issues, first save the results separately; do not fix the color first and then treat the link as an incidental result.
- Seeing only a match for `title` or `color` is not enough to show that `jquery.alerts.js` is responsible for generating attachments.
- If the page opens but the location is wrong, continue along the link branch; do not return to the attachment branch and rerun it.
- Without the original request body, you may record the observed behavior, but do not fill in pre-send fields.
- Without the caller version, retain the old-version judgment; do not change it into a conclusion about the current version.

These margin notes are more detailed than the first draft, but they do not present unconfirmed parts as conclusions that something is fixed. The current page remains an old troubleshooting entry point that can be consulted: it is suitable for routing by symptom, but cannot replace a review of the actual call relationships.

# Backtrace Link and Path Deduplication Decision

This record was initially treated as the shared entry point for two work items within a stable window. The reason it remains is not that shared implementation between the two work items has been confirmed, but that both earlier investigations began around the term “backtrace.” When this entry point continued to be used, the browser-side stack display, source links in reports, and path checks in the file tree could easily be connected into an imagined chain. This note therefore records the approaches compared at the time and retains the parts where the earlier judgment did not hold up.

The path first written at the top of the record was `public/javascripts/notifier.js`. The snippet that can be directly located at the frozen position is very small:

```javascript
function printStackTrace(options) {
  var ex = options.e || null, guess = !!options.guess;
}
```

This snippet shows that `printStackTrace(options)` accepts an options object, extracts the exception object, and reads the guessing flag. It is enough to explain why the earlier investigation started by looking at browser-side stack formatting; it does not indicate what kind of report the exception object came from, whether paths have already been deduplicated, or at which layer the source link is assembled. Earlier materials once turned “can jump to this file” into “the problem is mainly in this file.” These two statements should now be understood separately.

The original plan was to continue reading from notifier, while also looking for the causes of missing links and duplicate paths. This plan had one practical benefit: everyone had the same short entry point during discussions, and the historical record would not be scattered across two topics. However, it treated the reading entry point as the implementation owner. If we continued modifying things under this assumption, we might change display code because of inconsistencies in path inclusion and exclusion; we might also standardize file-tree checks in order to add source links. Neither action is supported by the existing material.

At the time, three ways of organizing the work were compared.

The first was to firmly bind both issues to this js file. It was the most convenient option, and the old records could immediately point to the same place. The cost was expanding the local information in `options.e` and `options.guess` into evidence for the entire backtrace chain. This approach was not adopted; the file location remains as legacy navigation, but is no longer considered the owner of changes to links or deduplication.

The second was to separate the topics completely by name and leave no shared record. This would avoid conceptual confusion, but would erase a piece of actual history: the two work items were indeed reviewed side by side within the same stable window, and the earlier investigation did indeed pass through notifier in both cases. If they were separated completely, people reading the old material later might mistakenly think they had never appeared under the same judgment. This approach was also not adopted.

The third was to keep this page and record the entry point they once shared and the shared-cause assumption that was overturned; executable verification would be documented separately. Source links should be checked only against the original report, source code, and the specific syntax units that were changed. Path deduplication should be checked only against the inclusion and exclusion results within the same file tree. The shared portion retains only navigation and misreading; it no longer represents shared implementation, shared change points, or shared verification results. This is the decision that remains.

The following sentence comes from an earlier judgment. It is no longer applicable, but is retained here to make it easier to verify old references:

> Starting from the stack function in notifier should reveal the causes of both the missing links and the duplicate paths.

The problem is not the act of starting by looking at notifier itself, but that it described the two phenomena under investigation as necessarily having a shared cause. The current reference points do not establish such a shared cause. It can be a reading assumption, but it can no longer be treated as a settled implementation judgment. Another abandoned inclination was to standardize path rules first and then see whether the links could be restored; that ordering likewise skipped the inputs that each side needs to confirm.

On the source-link side, TRC-222 is the verification entry point. This work requires running the source for “Mongoid backtrace source links” as-is against the current version and marking the specific syntax units that were changed. The focus here is the syntax and link location in the report, not guessing the link format from notifier variable names. The layer where the link is actually formed is not given by the existing material; therefore, “run as-is” is only a pending verification step and must not be written up as a result showing that the link has already been restored.

For path deduplication, TRC-226 serves as the entry point for verification. The scope is limited to comparing inclusion and exclusion results within the same file tree, without changing global user configuration. This restriction remains explicit: first let the local file tree provide the actual inclusion and exclusion results; configuration changes must not be used to mask differences in judgment. If the local comparison is inconsistent, simply record the included and excluded paths; do not recast it as a source-link compatibility issue, or invent shared rules to make the two topics appear connected.

The two review tracks branch off from the old entry point, rather than deriving an ordering dependency from it. This relationship can be viewed as follows:

```mermaid
stateDiagram-v2
  state "Old investigation entry point: notifier" as old_entry
  state "Source-link review" as link_check
  state "File-tree path comparison" as path_check
  [*] --> old_entry
  old_entry --> link_check
  old_entry --> path_check
  link_check --> [*]
  path_check --> [*]
```

The separation in the diagram is only the decision boundary for this page. It does not mean the two topics cannot intersect in the future, nor does it mean notifier has no relationship to either one; it only rejects using the current shared navigation as a substitute for a call relationship that has not yet been found. If a subsequent review does establish that both sides lead to the same section of implementation, that fact should be added separately, rather than retroactively making the old entry point bear the burden of proof.

Subsequent records show that TRC-222 had entered a processing state, after which the behavioral boundaries were reviewed using the frozen entry point for “Error Lifecycle and Fingerprints.” This review did not merge the two topics back into a single issue, nor did it provide evidence that notifier is the final implementation point for source links or path deduplication. What it changed was how the old material is read: the shared entry point returns to its navigation role, while the two work items each retain their own subject and scope of judgment.

The responsibility boundary also retains only two layers. Report source code, link locations, and changed syntax units fall within the verification scope of TRC-222; inclusion and exclusion within the same file tree fall within the verification scope of TRC-226. This page preserves the decision about why these two scopes must be separated. Where the source has not been traced to a specific function, an implementation owner or modification location should not be filled in here.

The remaining gaps have not disappeared as a result of this review: the existing reference points do not answer at which layer the source links in Mongoid reports are formed; the actual call sites involved in path deduplication have not been confirmed on this page either; whether `notifier.js` has any other related presentation responsibilities beyond serving as a convenient entry point for the old investigation still needs to be recorded separately in the corresponding work item. These gaps are the parts most easily overlooked when the old page continues to be cited.

Therefore, this page retains the historical practice of “starting from notifier and tracing back,” but no longer treats it as a unified fix approach. When the two topics appear side by side, first confirm whether you are checking report links or comparing file tree paths; similar names cannot substitute for call relationships.

# Decision on preserving the app cache vs. the original state

This discussion is not about rebuilding every old environment, but about deciding how to preserve the state we have. The two options are to keep using the fallback entry point or to separate problem aggregation from it. Both options retain the cache; the difference is whether subsequent reviews still treat them as the same kind of failure.

## Decision

Keep the current revision as the baseline for this inspection. Do not rebuild the environment to fill in the original state. Record problem aggregation separately and retain the fallback entry point, but no longer use it as a shared explanation for the two failure exits. This does not declare the cache equivalent to the original environment; it fixes the objects already observed so that new environment differences do not get mixed into the assessment before the original command is recovered.

## Rationale

In `docs/adj-app/decisions/app-quality-signal-Cache-vs-original-state-tradeoffs.md`, the fallback entry point and problem aggregation correspond to different failure exits. If both remain grouped under one entry point, aggregated samples will be recorded as fallback problems. Even with new failure samples later, we would not be able to tell whether a change occurred before the entry point or at aggregation.

Two pieces are still missing from the available material: the original command arguments have not been recovered, and the caller currently using the traceback line has not been confirmed. Neither gap provides grounds for an environment rebuild. Observations after a rebuild could come from the new environment rather than the revision at the time; continuing with the cache at least leaves the unresolved points where they were.

## Objections retained

The objection is that the cache will obscure the difference between reproducing in a single environment and rerunning in another environment; separating problem aggregation will also increase the number of records. This risk is valid, so the fallback entry point has not been deleted, nor has the aggregation record been made the sole new entry point. Both are retained side by side: the fallback entry point is for old values and rollback clues, while the aggregation record describes only its own failure exit.

For questions left by users, see DOC-32; this decision does not determine the caller's interpretation on their behalf. Once the original command arguments are recovered, or the traceback-line caller is confirmed, reassess whether the old entry point's priority needs to be restored. Until then, the current revision remains the cached state available for review.

Review trigger: compare entry-point priorities again only when both the original command arguments and the traceback-line caller have been recovered; if only one is recovered, continue retaining this cached state.
