# Cascade 4.2 Freeze Decision Record

This record preserves the choice made during the freeze window without flattening its distinctions. The discussion was not about reorganizing all notification paths, but about confirming whether the persistence entry point should move with Cascade 4.2, and what must be preserved first when an external hook fails. Beichen Operations Technology needed a decision that could be executed within the limits of the available material; call relationships that had not yet been reproduced could not substitute for the decision itself.

## The Two Options on the Table at the Freeze

**Keep the current persistence entry point.**

This option retained the entry point that could be found at the time, kept the scope of changes small, and allowed the existing path to remain a starting point for verification. Tracing back first led to `config/initializers/devise.rb`, but that was only a locating result. Being led there by the file location and call names did not prove that the file owned the entire behavior. The material also specifically placed `hook`, `rails`, `controller`, `model` and `client` on the same trace-back path, showing that the reviewers were concerned with behavioral branches after the entry point, rather than stopping at the initialization file.

**Adjust the window.**

This option sought to place the persistence entry point in the new window, reducing the time the old path would continue to exist. Its cost was not merely changing a location: if the entry point's actual scope of use had not yet been traced fully from the real Rails entry point, adjusting the window would carry forward observations and inferences that had not yet been separated. The freeze material did not provide reproduction results sufficient to cover this change, so it remained an option that had been compared, rather than becoming an action in this round.

The choice at the time was to keep the current persistence entry point and defer adjusting the window. Here, “keep” was a compatibility decision for the freeze period, not a judgment about permanent file ownership. If someone later located a different call boundary, that would not conflict with this decision; what would need to change was the window decision, rather than retroactively rewriting the early locating result as an incorrect fact.

## What the Meeting Material Actually Settled

When an external hook fails, first preserve the request body and status code. This requirement is narrower than “check whether the notification succeeded” and better reflects the situation on the ground. The request body preserves what the failing side actually sent, and the status code preserves the original result returned by the other end. Neither can be replaced by an imposed attribution of cause: seeing only the status code does not reveal the request content; saving only the request body does not establish whether the failure occurred during sending, receiving, or rejection by the other end.

The sequence adopted at the freeze was as follows:

```mermaid
flowchart LR
  A[Real Rails entry point] --> B[controller]
  B --> C[model]
  C --> D[decorator]
  D --> E[Notification client]
  E --> F[Preserve request body and status code on failure]
```

The arrows in the diagram indicate only the trace-back sequence required by the review, not proof that each layer necessarily calls the next. Anything directly visible in code or test output is recorded as an observation; anything deduced from an entry point's name, location, or call name is recorded as an inference. Mixing these two categories was an error this review repeatedly sought to avoid.

## Earlier Judgments Retained from the Initial Draft

The initial draft treated `config/initializers/devise.rb` as more of a stable ownership location than it is considered now. That wording was useful at the time because it provided a file that could be opened without inventing relationships between people or modules; however, it did not cover the path after the persistence entry point left the initialization file. The later follow-up tracing still produced no material proving that “entry point location” and “permanent ownership” were the same thing, so the earlier judgment remains in the record, with only its scope narrowed.

The initial draft also described adjusting the window as something that could be completed along the way during the freeze period. That judgment was not subsequently supported by the actual verification material. The verification record was only sufficient to show that both approaches remained under comparison; it could not justify describing the window adjustment as implemented, nor could “keep the current entry point” imply that all compatibility issues had disappeared. This caveat is not a new proposal; it merely prevents an earlier sentence from being read as a completed state.

The following matters were not combined into a single conclusion at the time:

| Subject recorded | What could be stated at the freeze | What could not simply be inferred |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `config/initializers/devise.rb` | One of the starting points for tracing back | The permanent ownership location for persistence |
| External hook failure | First preserve the request body and status code | The specific cause of the failure is already known |
| controller, model, decorator, client | The prescribed trace-back chain | Calls at every layer have been confirmed |
| Adjusting the window | An option that was compared | Already implemented within Cascade 4.2 |

The last column of the table marks where the assessment stopped at the time. It does not package unknowns as a specification; it preserves the boundaries of the evidence behind the decision. In particular, for hook failures, only preserving the request body and original status code makes it possible for the next verification to distinguish between “the request was sent but rejected” and “the request was not formed at an earlier layer.” These two situations were not merged at the freeze.

## Trade-offs After the Review

The direct benefit of keeping the current persistence entry point was avoiding simultaneous changes to the entry point and the compatibility window when evidence was insufficient. The existing material supported tracing downward from the real Rails entry point and saving the request body and status code on failure; it did not support a conclusion that a cross-layer adjustment was safe. The freeze decision therefore chose a smaller scope of action and left adjusting the window among the options not adopted.

This choice does not mean that the old entry point had no cost. Its continued existence means that subsequent verification must still address the relationships among the file location, controller, model, decorator, and notification client; looking only at `config/initializers/devise.rb` would again create the illusion that “we found the file, so the problem has been located.” The decision to retain the entry point accepted this cost in exchange for not expanding unverified changes during the freeze.

The sequence “adjust the window first, then add request records” was not adopted either. The request body and status code from an external hook failure are evidence from the incident itself; changing the window first would make it harder to compare the entry point where the failure occurred against the original records. The meeting material therefore placed saving the request body and status code at the beginning of failure handling, rather than treating it as an after-the-fact cleanup item. Here, “first” refers to processing order, not a judgment about the cause of failure.

## Verification Addendum

The actual verification added later did not provide enough detail to prove that adjusting the window had been adopted, nor did it elevate `config/initializers/devise.rb` to permanent ownership. Two points still stand: first, the real Rails entry point is the starting point for tracing back; second, the request body and status code are preserved first when an external hook fails. Other statements involving cross-layer calls continue to be separated into observations and inferences.

This version therefore does not present “verification” as a success report. Without new code snippets, test output, or status code samples, it does not fabricate a completed result. Nor does it entirely remove the earlier inclination, because that explains why the freeze decision kept the current entry point rather than directly proceeding with the window adjustment. A decision record needs to retain both the selected and unselected options; otherwise, readers will see only a current statement detached from the review context.

For the transition handoff of the notification integration on-call rotation, see DOC-44. Only the hook failure recording requirements connected to this freeze decision are retained here; the handoff content is not copied into this record.

## Objections Still Retained

The objection to adjusting the window was not that the window concept itself was unusable, but that the evidence at the time did not cover behavior after the entry point changed. Reproducing from the real Rails entry point first brings the issue back to the actual path; only by continuing through controller, model, decorator, and the notification client is there a chance to confirm the first branch. If this path is connected by names alone, adjusting the window would disguise a working hypothesis as a compatibility conclusion.

The objection to treating the initialization file as the final ownership location is also retained. A file can be a starting point for investigation, but it cannot by itself account for the full semantics of controller, model, decorator, and client. This objection and “keep the entry point for now during the freeze” can both hold: the former limits interpretation, while the latter limits changes. They are not two versions that overturn each other.

## Freeze Conclusion

Keep the current persistence entry point in this round; adjusting the window is not included in the freeze actions. When an external hook fails, first preserve the request body and status code. Start reproduction from the real Rails entry point, continue through controller, model, decorator, and the notification client to find the first branch, and record observations and inferences separately.

The scope of this conclusion ends here. It does not confirm permanent ownership of `config/initializers/devise.rb`, does not claim that adjusting the window has been completed, and does not fill in causes of failure that have not yet emerged for the next verification. Earlier proposals, earlier locating results, and caveats remain on file so that later assessments can understand why the scope of changes was not expanded during the freeze.

# Rechecking the Legacy Tracker in Notification Delivery

When taking over an issue around notification-delivery, the easiest mistake is to search directly for the adapter file based on the term “legacy tracker” and treat it as the entry point to the compatibility window. After review, that path can only serve as a starting point: the object provided by the delivery side and the object appearing on the adapter side have similar names, but that does not prove no conversion occurred between them, nor does it show that the compatibility check happened there.

This review follows a narrow path. Start at the repository entry notification-delivery and find one direct call site. At that call site, track only the object passed to the tracker. Do not fan out into the other delivery branches; follow this object to the first consumer that actually reads the compatibility state. Here, “consumer” means the location that reads the object state and uses it to decide whether the legacy interface is still available—not a wrapper layer that merely passes the object onward.

```text
        v
A direct call site

        v
The location where compatibility state is first read
        |
        v
The actual entry point to the legacy tracker compatibility window
```

The first call site is the most important anchor on this page. First check what it gives the tracker instead of guessing which adapter will eventually be called: if the object still carries runtime configuration there, the compatibility read later in the path can be compared against it; if the object has already been replaced with another representation, continuing to search by the delivery entry point's name will usually lead back to unrelated files. During review, inspect the object relationship before and after the call side by side. The goal is to confirm one transfer chain, not two local snippets that happen to have the same name.

`lib/issue_trackers/apis/unfuddle.rb` is still worth opening, but it belongs after this narrow path. Because of the tracker adapter's naming, this file was previously treated as the first candidate. On rechecking, it is better used as a signpost for confirming the object shape on the legacy adapter side: when the object passed down from the call site reaches the adapter area, this file can help identify that the tracker-related branch is being used. But the presence of API or “tracker” in the filename is not a reason to skip the call site and declare this the entry point to the compatibility window.

The configuration-loading trace answers a different question in this review. The delivery chain tells us where the object comes from; the configuration-loading trace tells us where the compatibility state carried by the object is populated. The two should not be conflated into one call edge. The investigation sequence can stay short: first fix the object for this run at notification-delivery, then confirm that the direct call site does not replace it; next, trace how the configuration enters the runtime object; only then look downstream for the first place that reads that state.

There is an easy-to-misread fork here. Some files contain terms for tracker, configuration, and the legacy interface at the same time, so they look like a complete answer. But if they do not receive the object passed from the previous hop, they are only nearby signposts. Recording these files is still useful, especially when the entry point needs to be rechecked next time; the current path does not continue through them. This also avoids mistaking every tracker adapter for a consumer of notification-delivery.

The initial draft placed `lib/issue_trackers/apis/unfuddle.rb` too close to the endpoint; that has now been corrected. It helps locate the adapter context but does not determine where compatibility state is first read. The actual entry point is based on the first location where the object is read. If that location only forwards configuration or wraps the request, continue to the next read point; if the read result already determines whether the legacy tracker still takes the compatibility branch, stop there and mark it as the actual entry point.

This review does not need to list every notification channel. The current object comes from notification-delivery, so retain only this delivery entry point and one direct call edge. Even if other channels eventually connect to the same tracker, each must be rechecked from its own entry point; this path cannot be applied across them.

The remaining boundary is where the object conversion occurs. The review so far confirms that the investigation should start from the call site rather than the adapter file, and distinguishes configuration population from compatibility-state reads. But whether a unified conversion has already happened before the call site still needs to be supplied by the owner responsible for constructing that part of the object. Once the answer is available, insert the conversion point between the first and second lines of the diagram above; there is no need to rewrite the locating rules that follow.

versions.body:
# Deployment Sample Discrepancy Review

During the deployment sample review window, the visible result did not match the original plan. The minimum notice payload was still present, but the corresponding display could not be directly explained by the notes left before the window. The window therefore did not continue treating the sample as a confirmation result as originally planned; the impact was limited to the judgment made in this review and was not generalized into a conclusion that the deployment path had failed.

## What Happened During the Window

- Once the review began, the first finding was that the sample's visible result did not match the expectation set during preparation.
- The first comparison did not immediately show whether the discrepancy was in the sample content, configuration, or deployment process. The original plan only specified what should be seen and left no record sufficient to trace back the point of change.
- The minimum notice payload from that time was then retained as a fixed input for revisiting the issue. It can only prove that this input was still present during the window; it cannot show which stage rewrote the result.
- Temporary restoration used the original configuration file. The rollback drill was run using the original configuration file, which was the control point added this time; after the drill was completed, the review could continue, but the restoration time was not treated as the time when the root cause had been established.
- Before the review ended, the sample returned to an observable state. The window record did not provide a repeatable attribution.

## Impact Assessment at the Time

During the shift, confirmation based on this sample was paused, and a display that looked normal was no longer treated as evidence that the original plan had been met. The other preparation items were not rechecked individually on this page. This was mainly to avoid misrecording the temporary restoration as proof that the sample itself was correct, not because a larger release issue had been confirmed.

The input left in the record was minimal; when reviewed later, it still allowed us to distinguish between “the sample exists” and “the sample result meets the plan.” The former was not lost during the window; the latter was not stably confirmed at the time.

## Earlier Assessment Retained

At the time, the discrepancy was tentatively attributed to an omission in sample preparation rather than to the deployment configuration itself. This assessment came from the surface result after restoration, not from ruling out the entire deployment process; the original record did not compare additional samples or break down the points of change one by one. This wording remains here to explain why the shift restored the review first, not as a conclusion for subsequent windows.

What remains unknown is whether the change that initially caused the visible result to diverge from the plan occurred in the sample, the configuration, or post-deployment processing; whether the minimum notice payload is sufficient to reproduce the same discrepancy in another window; and whether the rollback drill restored the display result or only restored the review entry point.

# Notification Rotation Result Troubleshooting Tree

The ticket says the notification integration on-call rotation is complete, but the result has no verifiable point of reference. Don’t branch first on whether the notification arrived; an email rendering appearing does not mean the rotation path was used.

```text
Inconsistent result
├─ Does presentation-mail’s invocation entry point match the version shown on the ticket?
│  ├─ No: Stop at the entry point and version; add the invocation record.
│  └─ Yes: Use the same input.
└─ Compare the configuration loading traces
   ├─ Different: Run the rollback drill using the original configuration file.
   └─ Same: Record the difference and stop here.
```

When the entry point and version match, use only the same input; do not switch the email content or configuration file. When comparing the configuration loading traces, record the loading order each side went through side by side. If the traces differ at all, run the rollback drill using the original configuration file; do not switch to the new configuration during the drill. If the traces are the same but the results still differ, record only the difference and the entry point at that time, then stop here. The next step requires new invocation evidence or someone who can clarify the rotation’s ownership; do not vote by repeatedly rerunning it.
